title: Dimensions, structure, and morphology variations of carbon-based materials for hydrogen storage: a review.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Introduction High research interest in the development of sustainable and efficient technology for energy storage is induced by a ubiquitous demand for energy and the established environmental crisis by the prevailing use of fossil fuels [ 1 ]. Hydrogen is of paramount interest as an alternative to conventional fossil fuels owing to its high energy density and carbon-free combustion products [ 2 ]. The hydrogen storage is one of the unwelcome issues in the development of hydrogen energy. Although hydrogen is an energy-intensive and environmentally benign energy carrier that holds great promise to meet long-term storage targets, the application of hydrogen will become stagnant unless impediments like its production, storage, and transportation are resolved [ 3 ]. Hydrogen storage conditions determine the energy cost of a method: the higher the hydrogen pressure and the difference between the storage temperature and the ambient temperature, the higher the energy cost. The optimal method should combine high hydrogen storage density with low energy consumption [ 4 ]. To pave the way to a practically viable hydrogen storage system, the low total mass of the storage system is essential [ 5 ,  6 ]. The underlying target of developing hydrogen storage materials is to enable their safe distribution to other sectors while also stronging usage as onboard fuel cell cars at ambient temperature. There are technical targets for onboard hydrogen storage systems set by three organizations, namely, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) (DOE, 2022), the Fuel Cells and Hydrogen Joint Undertaking (FCH JU) in Europe, and the New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO) (NEDO, 2015) in Japan. Based on these targets, the gravimetric density of hydrogen and cost should be around 6.5 wt% and 266 USD/kg (Table  1 ). Currently, no materials can meet the requirements. Table 1 Comparison of DOE targets in the US, FCH JU in Europe, and NEDO in Japan Targets Gravimetric density kWh/kg system (kg H 2 /kg) Volumetric density kWh/L system (kg H 2 /L system) Storage system cost $/kWh ($/kg H 2 ) DOE 2.2 (0.065) 1.7 (0.050) $8 ($266) FCH JU 1.2 (0.035) 2 (0.060) $10.40 ($338) NEDO 2.5 (0.075) 2.36 (0.071) $5.4 ($180) Creating a storage technology that is competitive, compact, and ecologically sustainable will enhance the ability of hydrogen to rival natural and synthetic fuels in the market effectively. At present, the most widely utilized and commercially available hydrogen storage technologies are compressed gas and liquid storage. However, there is a rapidly growing interest in emerging solid-state hydrogen storage materials as alternative solutions. Hydrogen can be implemented into porous materials or metal hydrides via chemisorption and physicochemical or physisorption interactions [ 7 ]. While chemisorption interaction, which mainly occurs in metal hydrides, is based on a vigorous reaction with hydrogen molecules [ 7 ], physisorption (porous materials such as zeolites, MOFs, activated carbon, and other carbon-based materials) occurs through weak and long-range interactions. Thus, physical–chemical interaction is considered the most pertinent for the development of solid hydrogen storage materials because, according to DOE [ 7 ], it requires an appropriate range of temperature (− 40 to 85 °C) and pressure (< 100 atm) for on-board purposes. Carbon materials are highly promising for hydrogen storage due to their high stability, low cost, and scalability. However, their reliance on physisorption limits their hydrogen storage capacity at ambient conditions compared to chemisorption-based materials like metal and complex hydrides. Among the porous materials extensively studied, MOFs and COFs stand out due to their tunable structures, high crystallinity, and consistent synthesis processes [ 8 ]. Their exceptionally high surface area makes them particularly appealing for hydrogen storage applications. Additionally, MOFs offer unique merits through the presence of metal binding sites and the ability to post-synthetically modify linkers, setting them apart from other porous materials. However, a significant drawback of MOFs, COFs, and porous polymers like PIMs lies in their limitations. Despite their high surface area, these materials often suffer from relatively poor chemical and thermal stability, as well as obstacles in achieving sustainable large-scale synthesis [ 8 ]. In contrast, porous carbon presents a cost-effective alternative. It can be synthesized more easily on an industrial scale and derived from recyclable, carbon-rich waste materials, comprising bio-based precursors. Recently, porous carbons have garnered significant attention due to their numerous advantages over other materials. Their superior chemical and thermal stability compared to MOFs and porous polymers, along with a wide range of optimization strategies to enhance hydrogen storage capacity, make them a promising choice for practical applications. Due to their unique geometry, super conductivity, and adjustable micro-structure, functional carbon materials have been extensively introduced into hydrogen storage systems as host materials, barrier layers, and catalyzers. In addition, considerable attention has been given to carbon-based materials owing to their low cost, low weight, high surface area, high chemical stability, morphologies variations, and specific interaction between gas molecules and carbon atoms as potential hydrogen storage materials [ 9 ]. Carbon-based materials can densely pack the hydrogen gas molecules with protection and persistence. Figure  1  reveals their advantages and disadvantages. Fig. 1 Scheme of pros and cons of carbon materials applied for hydrogen storage systems It is well known that a hydrogen molecule forms a link with a typical carbon-based arrangement by mild van der Waals interactions, with an energy range of 0.04 to 0.12 eV [ 10 ]. In this case, most carbon atoms are in sp 2  hybridization. In contrast, when a hydrogen atom reacts chemically with a carbon atom, orbital hybridization shifts from sp 2  to sp 3 , producing a binding energy between 2 and 3 eV Fig.  2 . Fig. 2 The hybridization of carbon in the graphene sheet Moreover, a computational study has shown that graphene or carbon nanotubes have the potential to be used as hydrogen storage materials [ 11 ]. Earlier studies reported that the higher electron affinity of carbon nanoparticles depends on the structure of carbon-based materials. As demonstrated in Fig.  3 , a higher number of pores, folding, and angles, and higher electron affinity make the Desorption of hydrogen easier [ 12 ]. Fig. 3 Correlation of electron affinity and hydrogen removal energy (adopted from [ 12 ]) Carbon atoms can form covalent bonds with three, five, or seven adjacent carbon atoms, potentially creating pentagonal and heptagonal surfaces. These surface configurations facilitate the presence of intricate solids and large molecules like activated carbon, graphite, diamond, carbon nanofibers, fullerene structures, single-wall nanotubes, and multi-wall nanotubes. Cutting-edge science and engineering are enabling the synthesis of a range of nanostructured carbon materials, comprising zero-dimensional (NPs, fullerenes, quantum dots) [ 13 – 15 ], 1-dimensional (carbon nanotubes (single-walled carbon nanotubes, multiwalled carbon nanotubes), carbon nanofibers) [ 16 – 18 ], 2-dimensional (graphene sheets) [ 19 – 22 ] and 3-dimensional (carbon nano-onions, carbon nanospheres, mesoporous carbon) [ 23 – 25 ] structures etc. have aroused great interest in the research community due to their unique structural properties as shown in Fig.  4 . In Fig.  5 , the steps in carbon materials modification implemented in hydrogen storage systems ranging from the twentieth century up to present days are described [ 26 – 30 ]. Currently, novel hybrid structures are based on a combination of materials with distinct morphologies and dimensions [ 31 ]. Fig. 4 Schematic for the molecular models of carbon nanostructures Fig. 5 Scheme of the early development of carbon-based materials for hydrogen storage systems This review highlights the carbon materials with different morphological structure dimensionalities from 0 to 3D that are under investigation, encompassing the synthesis procedures and their structure-related hydrogen storage performances when applied as hydrogen storage material. This is followed by a discussion of current approaches and strategies for enhancing hydrogen storage properties using carbon-derived substances. The features of 0D, 1D, 2D, and 3D carbonaceous materials are also mentioned with examples. This review aims to accentuate the critical importance of dimensionality and morphological structure, thus investigating their influence on carbon materials design applied in hydrogen storage systems.
